Standardised incidence ratio, with an exact interval

Source: R/areal.R
stdinc.Rd

Divides each area's observed count by its expected count to give the standardised incidence ratio (SIR), and adds an exact Poisson confidence interval. A ratio of one is the overall experience; above one is an excess and below one a deficit. Use it after expcnts to say which areas differ from the overall rate by more than chance.

Usage

stdinc(obs, expd, area = NULL, conflvl = 0.95)

Arguments

obs

Numeric vector of observed counts (non-negative).

expd

Numeric vector of expected counts (positive), for example from expcnts; the same length as obs, or length one.

area

Optional vector of area labels, added as the first column. Default NULL.

conflvl

Number in (0, 1), default 0.95: the two-sided confidence level of the interval.

Value

A data frame with one row per area: area (when given), observed, expected, sir, lower, upper (numeric), and logical excess (the interval lies above one), deficit (the interval lies below one) and significant (either).

Details

With observed count \(O\) and expected \(E\), \(SIR = O / E\). The interval for \(1 - \alpha\) coverage is $$\left[\frac{G^{-1}(\alpha/2;\, O)}{E},\ \frac{G^{-1}(1-\alpha/2;\, O+1)}{E}\right]$$ where \(G^{-1}(p; k)\) is the gamma quantile with shape \(k\); the lower limit is 0 when \(O = 0\). This is the exact Poisson interval, from the relation between the Poisson and gamma distributions, and so is identical to stats::poisson.test()'s. It is the interval to use here because the counts that matter are small: a normal approximation on an observed count of three is not an interval, it is a decoration.

Each area's interval is a separate test; with many areas some will exclude one by chance (see scanadj). Missing values are dropped before the lengths are compared.

Errors: negative, infinite or non-numeric counts; an expected count of zero or below; lengths that differ (a single expd is recycled). A conflvl outside (0, 1) is an error.

References

Lawson, A. B. Using R for Bayesian Spatial and Spatio-Temporal Health Modeling. Chapman and Hall/CRC, Chapter 1.

See also

expcnts, ebrates, fnllim

Examples

stdinc(obs = c(30, 12, 3), expd = c(20, 14, 5),
    area = c("North", "South", "East"))
#>    area observed expected       sir     lower    upper excess deficit
#> 1 North       30       20 1.5000000 1.0120437 2.141343   TRUE   FALSE
#> 2 South       12       14 0.8571429 0.4428982 1.497256  FALSE   FALSE
#> 3  East        3        5 0.6000000 0.1237344 1.753455  FALSE   FALSE
#>   significant
#> 1        TRUE
#> 2       FALSE
#> 3       FALSE

# An observed count of three carries almost no information, and the
# interval says so rather than hiding it.
stdinc(3, 5)
#>   observed expected sir     lower    upper excess deficit significant
#> 1        3        5 0.6 0.1237344 1.753455  FALSE   FALSE       FALSE

# a 90 percent interval, and a zero count (lower limit exactly 0)
stdinc(c(0, 40), c(2, 25), conflvl = 0.90)
#>   observed expected sir   lower    upper excess deficit significant
#> 1        0        2 0.0 0.00000 1.497866  FALSE   FALSE       FALSE
#> 2       40       25 1.6 1.20783 2.082775   TRUE   FALSE        TRUE

try(stdinc(c(3, 4), c(5, 0)))
#> Error : stdinc: `expd` must be positive
